legend: After learning about polynomial hashing, Heidi decided to learn about shift-xor hashing. In particular, she came across this interesting problem.

Given a bitstring y∈{0,1}n$$$y \in \{0,1\}^n$$$ find out the number of different k$$$k$$$ (0≤k<n$$$0 \leq k  \lt  n$$$) such that there exists x∈{0,1}n$$$x \in \{0,1\}^n$$$ for which y=x⊕shiftk(x).$$$y = x \oplus \mbox{shift}^k(x).$$$

In the above, ⊕$$$\oplus$$$ is the xor operation and shiftk$$$\mbox{shift}^k$$$ is the operation of shifting a bitstring cyclically to the right k$$$k$$$ times. For example, 001⊕111=110$$$001 \oplus 111 = 110$$$ and shift3(00010010111000)=00000010010111$$$\mbox{shift}^3(00010010111000) = 00000010010111$$$.
input: The first line contains an integer n$$$n$$$ (1≤n≤2⋅105$$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$), the length of the bitstring y$$$y$$$.
The second line contains the bitstring y$$$y$$$.
output: Output a single integer: the number of suitable values of k$$$k$$$.
note: There is no x$$$x$$$ such that x⊕x=1010$$$x \oplus x = 1010$$$, hence the answer is 3$$$3$$$.
